actions.body: The pursuit of autonomous scientific inquiry requires more than just processing power; it demands a structured way to ask: 'What should I do next?' Our synthesis indicates that computational creativity is best viewed through a modular lens—problem formulation, representation, manipulation, and evaluation. This isn't just theory; we see these components at work in human-like problem solving and particle physics outreach models. Crucially, recent work in active inference suggests that the friction of making these choices—cognitive effort—is actually the engine that drives an agent to switch from simple habit to deeper, optimal discovery. Summary: Machines need structured evaluation frameworks and cognitive effort management to move from simple instruction-following to autonomous scientific inquiry.
actions.lede: How do machines learn to care about new problems when no one is watching?
actions.reason: Disseminating the findings on modular creativity frameworks and the role of cognitive effort in autonomous goal-setting.
actions.title: Navigating Autonomous Creativity

review.alternative: Emergent, non-decomposable creative processes as opposed to modular frameworks.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence of high-performing creative agents lacking these identifiable modular components.

claims.statement: Computational creativity frameworks necessitate a structured decomposition into four components: problem formulation, knowledge representation, manipulation, and evaluation.

support.explanation: This establishes the foundational modular requirement for autonomous creative systems.
support.passage: Our framework consists of four main components of a CPS problem, namely, 1) problem formulation, 2) knowledge representation, 3) method of knowledge manipulation, and 4) method of evaluation.

review.alternative: Cognitive effort as purely informational gain or uncertainty reduction without habit-conflict dynamics.
review.would_change_mind: Data showing agent performance is invariant to policy-habit conflict levels.

claims.statement: Cognitive effort, modeled as the cost of resolving conflicts between habits and optimal policies, is a critical variable in autonomous problem-solving performance.

support.explanation: This mechanism links agent decision-making dynamics (drift-diffusion) to high-level policy conflict resolution.
support.passage: High-level theories rooted in the Bayesian Brain Hypothesis often frame cognitive effort as the cost of resolving the conflict between habits and optimal policies.

actions.findings:

actions.limitations: Current findings rely on theoretical models and existing computational surveys rather than deployment in fully autonomous open-ended scientific laboratories. Integration of high-level cognitive models with agent-specific architectural constraints remains limited.
actions.next_questions: How do self-modifying agents adapt their internal evaluation criteria in response to failure without external guidance?
actions.reason: Incorporating active inference mechanisms into the existing problem-solving framework enhances the structural understanding of how agents identify and prioritize novel problems.
actions.summary: Autonomous problem formulation relies on decomposing tasks into formulation, representation, manipulation, and evaluation components, while cognitive effort—mediated by active inference and drift-diffusion mechanisms—governs the transition between habitual behaviors and optimal policies.
